newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany vows to play by rules, still enter EMU.
newsitem.headline: Germany vows to play by rules, still enter EMU.

text.p: A senior German government official on Tuesday stressed Bonn's commitment to Europe's currency union, insisting it would play by the rules laid out in the Maastricht Treaty and still meet key entry criteria.

Shrugging off growing talk Germany, which sees itself as the driving force behind European integration, may be shut out in 1999, Juergen Stark, state secretary in Bonn's finance ministry, insisted Bonn would meet the deficit criteria.

"I think that with the newest numbers which we have put together, the 2.9 percent budget deficit ratio (as compared with gross domestic product) we will fulfil the Maastricht Treaty deficit criteria," he told a banking forum.
The 2.9 percent figure already included provisions for higher unemployment rates, which in January soared to 4.7 million people, marking the highest level seen since the 1930s, Stark said.
But he also underscored that Germany still had a tough road ahead, saying "We still need to do our homework."
Stark however declined to say whether this could include a spending freeze, saying he did not know whether such action, which has been widely talked about, would be implemented.

Acknowledging the German public's fears about giving up the mark, Stark said the planned union's foundations were strong enough to allow the new currency, the euro, to successfully take over the mark's role as a major world currency.

"A hard euro will provide an equally strong alternative to the dollar," Stark said, adding "in all areas the euro will assume the mark's role and, because of the greater economic potential, actually expand on these."
But Stark also left no doubts that the euro could be strong only if all nations, wishing to adopt it, presented durably low budget deficits and government debt.
"A nation will not gain entry into the currency union by meeting stability oriented average standards but rather only by ascending to the top standard," Stark said.
Although the Maastricht Treaty left room for some interpretation of the criteria, Stark stressed, "We cannot and do not want to use this room for interpretation."
While Stark praised nations' broad efforts to consolidate finances, he also worried that certain nations might not yet be ready to sustain such programmes permanently.

"My worry is that during this race to catch up some unrealistic goals will be set and that an economy's short-term, ability to make adjustments will not be taken into account sufficiently," Stark said.

Just one day after Italy lashed out at Germany for failing to tackle its current problems, Stark stopped short of returning fire, assuring that Germany was not involved in any plan to keep Italy out of the currency union at the start.

Referring to reports German officials were conspiring to exclude Italy, Stark said, "There are no such plans, at least if there is work being done on such a plan it is not being done with Germany's participation."
Trying to smoothe ruffled diplomatic feathers, Stark insisted "I cannot say who will qualify, and of course we are interested in having as many nations as possible enter." 182147 GMT feb 97
